title: The Lost Kitten
author: Lexicon Stories
description: Девочка находит маленького серого котёнка и хочет вернуть его хозяевам. Простая тёплая история о доброте и новых друзьях.
paragraphs: One rainy morning, Mia heard a small sound outside her door. "Meow, meow," said the sound. Mia opened the door and saw a little grey kitten. It was wet and cold, and it was very afraid.
"Oh, poor kitten!" said Mia. "Come inside. You can be warm here."
The kitten walked slowly into the house. Mia gave it a warm towel and some milk. The kitten drank all the milk and closed its eyes. Soon it was sleeping on the soft towel.

Mia wanted to find the kitten's home. Maybe somebody lost their kitten. She drew a picture of the kitten on paper. She wrote: "Found: a little grey kitten. Please call Mia." She put the pictures on the street, on the trees and on the shop door.
Two days passed. Nobody called. The kitten was happy in Mia's house. It played with a ball of wool. It slept on Mia's bed. Mia gave it a name: Smokey, because it was grey like smoke.
On the third day, the phone rang. "Hello," said an old man. "I saw your picture. My wife and I lost our kitten, Leo. He is grey with white paws."
Mia looked at the kitten. It had small white paws! "Yes," she said. "I have a grey kitten with white paws."
The old man and his wife came to Mia's house in the afternoon. When the old woman saw the kitten, she started to cry. "Leo! Our little Leo!" The kitten ran to her and jumped on her lap.
But then the kitten walked back to Mia and sat near her feet.
The old woman smiled. "It seems Leo likes you too," she said. "Can we be friends? You can visit Leo every week."
"Yes, please!" said Mia.
And that is how Mia found a kitten and made two new friends. Now every Friday she visits Leo — and Leo always waits for her at the window.

title: The Magic Paintbrush
author: Lexicon Stories
description: Бедный мальчик Том получает волшебную кисточку: всё, что он рисует, становится настоящим. Но кисточка работает только для добрых рук.
paragraphs: Tom lived in a small house at the end of the village. He was poor, but he had a big heart. Every evening he drew pictures in the sand with a stick. He drew the sun, the sea and birds in the sky.
One night, somebody knocked on the door. An old woman stood there. Her clothes were old, but her eyes were kind.
"I like your pictures," she said. "Here is a paintbrush for you. Use it well." She gave Tom a golden paintbrush and walked away. In the dark sky, Tom saw a small light, and then the woman was gone.
In the morning, Tom tried the brush. He painted an apple on the old wall — and the apple became real! He took it in his hand. It was red and fresh. He ate it and laughed with happiness.

Then Tom painted bread for the hungry children near the river. The bread became real, and the children ate it. He painted shoes for a boy with no shoes. He painted a warm coat for the old fisherman. Every day he painted something for people, and every day the village was a little happier.
But a rich man in the village heard about the brush. "Paint me a mountain of gold!" he said to Tom. "No," said Tom. "This brush helps people. It does not make gold for greedy men."

At night, the rich man took the brush from Tom's house. In the morning, he painted a mountain of gold. Nothing happened. He painted gold coins, bags, rings — only paint. The brush did not work. The brush worked only for kind hands.
The rich man was very angry. He threw the brush into the river and went home with no gold.
But the river was kind too. In the morning, Tom found the brush near his door, wet and shining in the sun.
Tom smiled, took his brush and painted a big yellow sun over the village. That morning, the long winter ended, the snow started to melt, and everybody in the village smiled too.

title: The Winter Fox
author: Lexicon Stories
description: Нина каждый день ходит в школу через лес и замечает худую молодую лису. Она начинает приносить ей хлеб, и между ними рождается необычная дружба.
paragraphs: Nina walked to school through the forest every day. It was December, and the forest was white and quiet. She liked this walk more than the noisy bus.
One cold morning, she saw a fox near the big pine trees. It was young and very thin. The fox looked at Nina with sad yellow eyes, and then it disappeared between the trees.
At school, Nina could not stop thinking about the fox. There was almost no food in the forest in winter. So the next morning, she put a piece of bread in her bag.

The fox was there again, near the same pines. Nina put the bread on a stone, took three steps back and waited. The fox came slowly, took the bread and ran away. It happened so fast that Nina laughed out loud.

After that, Nina brought bread every day. The fox was afraid at first, but every morning it came a little closer. By the end of January, it ate from the stone while Nina stood two metres away. She started to talk to it about school, the weather and her homework. The fox listened and moved its ears.
"You need a name," Nina said one day. "I will call you Ember, because of your red coat."
In March, Ember stopped coming. Nina looked for her every morning, but the forest was empty. She was sad, but she understood: winter was over, and wild animals do not need bread in spring.
Then, on a warm day in May, Nina walked home through the forest and heard a strange sound in the grass. She stopped.

Ember came out of the bushes — and behind her walked three small fox cubs. They had the same red coats and the same curious eyes. Ember looked at Nina, as if she wanted to say: "Look. I want you to meet my family."
The cubs were not afraid. One of them tried to play with Nina's shoelace.

Nina did not give them bread anymore — they were strong hunters now, and the forest was full of food. But every May, when she walked to school, three young foxes ran near the path with her for a few metres, and one old red fox watched them from the pine trees.
Wild animals do not say thank you. But Nina knew that Ember remembered.

title: The Last Bus Home
author: Lexicon Stories
description: Бен опаздывает на последний автобус после тренировки и идёт домой пешком. По дороге он встречает пожилую женщину, и эта прогулка меняет его отношение ко многим вещам.
paragraphs: Ben ran to the bus stop as fast as he could, but it was too late. The red tail lights of the last bus disappeared around the corner. He stood there with his football bag and did not know what to do. It was nine o'clock in the evening, and his home was four kilometres away.
He had no money for a taxi. His phone was dead. His mother worked until ten. There was only one thing to do: walk.
"Great," he said angrily. "Just great."
He walked past the shops, past the school and past the park. At the next bus stop, he saw an old woman with two heavy shopping bags. She looked at the empty road, then at Ben.
"Did we miss it?" she asked.
"Yes," said Ben. "The last bus just left."
"Oh dear," said the woman. "I do not like walking in the dark, but I do not like waiting here either."
Ben thought for a second. He was tired and angry, but she was old, and her bags looked really heavy. "I can carry your bags," he said. "And we can walk together. It is safer."
The woman smiled. "Thank you, young man. My name is Edith."
"I'm Ben."

They walked slowly along the quiet street. Edith told him about the town many years ago, when there was a cinema on Green Street and an ice cream café near the bridge. Ben told her about football and his dog. Without noticing, he stopped being angry about the bus.
"You know," said Edith, "my daughter always tells me to take a taxi. But I like the bus. On the bus, you meet people."
When they turned into Mill Street, Ben stopped. "Wait. You live on Mill Street? I live at number fourteen!"
Edith laughed. "I live at number nine. We are neighbours, and I have never seen you before. Young people always run somewhere."
At Edith's door, Ben carried the bags up her steps. Before closing the door, she said: "Next time, Ben, we will miss the bus together, and you will tell me about your matches."
Ben walked the last thirty metres to his door and smiled in the dark. The evening that started so badly became one of his favourite evenings.
Now, when he sees the old woman at the bus stop, he always sits next to her. The last bus is fine. But the walk is better.

title: The Key to Number Nine
author: Lexicon Stories
description: После смерти дедушки Сэм получает в наследство старый ключ и записку с загадочным адресом «Number Nine». Поиски приводят его к части семейной истории, о которой никто не рассказывал.
paragraphs: The lawyer gave Sam a small box after the funeral. Inside there was an old brass key and a piece of paper in his grandfather's handwriting. The paper said only: "Number Nine. It is still yours."
Sam's grandfather had never talked much about his past: a small town by the sea, a mechanic's job, a love of chess. Nothing about any number nine.
Why leave a key without an address? Sam decided to solve the mystery before the weekend.

In his grandfather's old letters in the attic, Sam found a photograph: a group of young men in front of a building with a wide wooden door. On the back, somebody had written: "The club, 1962". The street sign was not readable, but the number on the door looked like a nine.

At the town archive, an archivist with grey hair studied the photograph and smiled. "That is Station Road," she said, checking an old map. "Number nine was the Sea Cadets hall. It closed in the eighties."

The hall was still standing. The old wooden door had been replaced by a metal one, and Sam's brass key clearly belonged to the wooden door. He stood there for a while, feeling that the trail was going cold.

At home, he posted the photograph in a town history group on the internet. On Friday evening his phone exploded with notifications. An elderly man had replied: "I know this door. I was one of those boys. Your grandfather — he taught me chess!"

They met on Saturday. The old man, Mr. Wilson, explained everything. In the sixties, the boys had a secret place behind the main hall — a small storage room called "the workshop", hidden behind the stage. Each member of the club received a brass key when he was ready to keep the club's memory. Before he moved away, Sam's grandfather had promised that the workshop would never be forgotten. He was the last one who kept a key.
The metal door of the hall was locked too, but Mr. Wilson knew the caretaker. Twenty minutes later, Sam stood behind the stage, in front of a small wooden door with a scratched brass lock.

His hands were shaking a little when the key turned. Inside the dusty room he found a chessboard set up in the middle of a game — the same game they had started to play more than sixty years ago. Beside the board lay a notebook with a list of names. The last line was empty.
Sam took out a pen and wrote his name under his grandfather's. Then he sat down on the old stool and made the next move for the white pieces.
"Check," he said quietly to the empty room, and for the first time in weeks, he smiled for real.

title: The Photograph
author: Lexicon Stories
description: Элли находит старую фотографию, забытую в библиотечной книге, и решает вернуть её владельцам. Помощь незнакомцу превращается в историю о разлучённых брате и сестре.
paragraphs: Ellie found the photograph on a rainy Tuesday, between pages 214 and 215 of an old library book about shipping. It showed a young man and a young woman on a train platform, and on the back somebody had written: "Me and Kath. The day she left. 1963. Find her again one day — A."
The book had not been taken out since 1998. Somebody had kept the photo inside it — and forgotten it for a quarter of a century.
Ellie worked at the library, so she checked the old handwritten reader's card. The name was almost impossible to read, but it looked like "A. Merrick".
Instead of leaving it in the lost property drawer, she posted it on the town's community page: "Found in a library book. Does anyone know Arthur and Kath?"
The post got forty comments in the first evening. But one, which arrived at midnight, was different: "My father is Arthur Merrick. Why are you asking about my father?"

They talked on the phone the next morning. Arthur was eighty-four and lived in a nursing home nearby. His son, David, explained carefully: his father almost never spoke about his youth, except for one strange habit. Every year, on the same autumn day, he wrote a postcard to an address in Canada that nobody could find.

"Kath was his younger sister," David said. "She emigrated in 1963. They promised to write. The first letters arrived, and then the family moved houses, and the letters stopped. There was no internet then, and the trail went cold."
That weekend David took the photograph to the nursing home. His father held it for a long time without saying a word.

Ellie could not stop thinking about it. Searching for people was not her job, but she was patient, and the internet was something the Merricks of 1963 had never had. She found a "Kathleen Merrick" in British Columbia, born in 1945, still teaching piano in 2019 — still alive, with a public email address.
She called David before writing anything. "Just show her the photo first," she said. "Let it be theirs."

A week later, David called from the nursing home. He did not say much: his father had wept, which nobody had seen in years, and the letter to Canada had finally been posted, with a real address and a real stamp.

The reply came in December. Kathleen was eighty, her memory sharp. The first sentence of her letter was: "I thought you were angry with me all these years. I wrote to the old house every Christmas until the letters came back."

They video-called in January, and Ellie was invited too. She watched from the edge of the screen as two white-haired people laughed at a tiny photograph of two young ones on a platform, half a century and an ocean apart.
The library book about shipping still sits on its shelf. And Ellie now checks every returned book for forgotten things, twice.

title: The New Neighbour
author: Lexicon Stories
description: Диалоговая история: Анна знакомится с новым соседом Марком, который переехал в город и не знает в нём никого. Разговор у двери заканчивается чаем и первым другом на новом месте.
paragraphs: Anna was carrying shopping bags up the stairs when she saw a man standing in front of the flat next to hers. He had a box in his hands and an address label on his sleeve.
"Hello! Are you moving in?" asked Anna.
"Yes, I am," said the man. "I'm Mark. I moved in yesterday, but the door key doesn't work. I have been standing here for twenty minutes."

"Oh no! Let me look at the label. Hmm, this is the key from the street door, not from your flat. The number is the same, that's why it's confusing. The landlady lives on the first floor. She has the right key."
"Thank you! I didn't know that. This town is new for me — I arrived two days ago."
"Where are you from?"
"From Leeds. I found a job here, in the hospital."
"A doctor?"
"No, a cook, in the hospital kitchen. I like cooking. But I don't know anybody in this town yet."
"Then you are lucky," Anna laughed. "I'm Anna, from flat five. I know everybody. Do you need help with your boxes?"
"Really? You have your hands full already."
"These bags are for my grandmother, she lives downstairs. Wait, I'll leave them at her door and come back. Where are the rest of your boxes?"
"In the taxi downstairs. The driver went to find a parking place an hour ago. I think I need to call him."
"Don't worry, we'll manage. There is a trolley in the basement. I'll show you."
They carried the boxes together. Mark had a lot of books, a small TV and a big green plant.
"A lemon tree!" said Anna. "My grandmother has one too. Hers is twenty years old."
"Mine is three. It gave one lemon last year. One!"
"Then it needs time. Listen, we are making a cake on Sunday for my grandmother's birthday. Would you like to come? You can taste real home cooking."
"I would love to. Maybe I can bake something too?"
"Can you bake?"
"Apple pie. It's the only thing I can bake, but I'm very good at it."
"A cook and a baker! Perfect. Sunday, at four o'clock, flat five."

In the evening, Mark stood in his kitchen, in the middle of the boxes, and made tea. The flat was still strange and the walls were empty, but the kettle was old and kind — it had come from his grandmother's house in Leeds — and somewhere on the other side of the wall, his new neighbour was probably doing the same thing.
"Not a bad first day," he said to the lemon tree. The lemon tree said nothing, but on the windowsill the last yellow lemon looked almost ready to pick.
On Sunday, the apple pie was a great success. Grandmother said it was the best pie in town, and Mark wrote the recipe in his small blue notebook, on the first page.

title: The Signal
author: Lexicon Stories
description: Радиолюбитель Мара ловит странный повторяющийся сигнал с маяка, который закрыли сорок лет назад. Расследование приводит её к традиции, которую кто-то продолжает до сих пор.
paragraphs: In six years as a radio amateur, Mara had never heard anything like it. It was the night of the autumn storm, the kind that knocked out the internet and made the valley quiet. Then, between two bursts of static on 4,652 kHz — a frequency where nobody should be transmitting — a signal appeared.

It was Morse code, slow and patient, repeated again and again. Mara wrote the letters down by hand. The message made no sense: NORTH. STORM. SAFE. HOME. — and then a line that made her sit up straight: GREETINGS TO ALL SHIPS AT SEA. THIS IS CAPE MERROW LIGHT.
The Cape Merrow lighthouse had been closed for forty years — a white tower on the rocks, a tourist photo spot.
The signal repeated for exactly nine minutes and then disappeared.

The next day, Mara looked for a rational explanation. Old equipment restarting itself was a theory, but the message was too clean, too modern — and the pauses between words were just a little too long, like a speaker choosing words carefully.

Three weeks later, another storm came, and with it the signal. Same frequency, same nine minutes. This time Mara was ready. The word list had changed, and a new line had been added: FOR THOSE WHO LISTEN — YOU ARE NOT ALONE OUT THERE.

That sentence made her take a day off work. Two hours along the coastal path brought her to Cape Merrow. The tower stood dark and fenced, but on the keeper's cottage she noticed a small solar panel and a cable running inside through a broken window.

The cottage door was unlocked. Inside, in the dust, stood a table with a low-power transmitter, a brass key and a notebook. Above it hung a photograph of a keeper with careful handwriting underneath: "Thomas Erry, keeper of this light, 1954–1986. Every storm, he greeted the ships and told them: you are not alone."

The last page of the notebook was written in a different, female hand: "My father sent his greetings for thirty years. The light is off, but the habit of kindness is not a lamp. If you have heard this message: come and send it with me. — Ruth Erry."
Mara wrote her name and her call sign in the notebook, under eleven other names going back years.
She was cleaning the brass key when a woman of about sixty appeared in the doorway with two thermoses.
"You're not the electricity inspector," the woman said.
"I'm the new name in your notebook," said Mara. "I heard the storm message. Is it true I can send it too?"
Ruth Erry laughed for the first time in a long time and handed her one of the thermoses.
That night, when the next squall hit the coast, two operators sat at the little table, and the signal went out to sea again: NORTH. STORM. SAFE. HOME. YOU ARE NOT ALONE OUT THERE.
At sea, Mara liked to think, somebody heard it.
